newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Five S.Korean companies allowed to invest in North.
newsitem.headline: Five S.Korean companies allowed to invest in North.

text.p: South Korea on Friday allowed five local companies to invest in North Korea as part of a drive to seek detente and build mutual trust, the National Unification Ministry said.

The move, which also allows a telecommunications company to pursue a joint project with a North Korean partner, comes only four days before the two Koreas are due to hold talks along with the United States and China.
The five include Samsung Electronics Co, South Korea's largest electronics company, and Kolon International, a leading manufacturer of textile products, a ministry statement said.
The other companies are apparel and food processing companies.

"These steps are taken in accordance with the government's consistent policy to increase economic exchanges and cooperation to achieve reconciliation between the South and North and build up mutual trust," it said.
Next Tuesday, senior officials of the two Koreas, the United States and China are due to meet in New York to set a date, venue and agenda for four-nation peace talks.

The four-party talks, first proposed by U.S. President Bill Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam in April 1996, are aimed at hammering out a permanent peace settlement to replace the armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.

Seoul officials have said large-scale economic assistance to the impoverished North could be discussed during the peace talks if Pyongyang is willing to take steps to ease tensions on the Korean peninsula, the last Cold War flashpoint.
The companies approved to seek investment can explore business opportunities in North Korea but they need separate approval from the Seoul government before investing cash in the communist state.
Friday's move brings to 20 the number of South Korean firms that have been allowed to pursue business in the North.
"Our government will seriously consider any further applications from local companies depending on the development of inter-Korean relations and North Korea's attitude," the ministry statement said.

Of the 20 companies, only two have so far invested in the North for joint ventures. They are Daewoo Corp's $5.12 million investment in a clothing maker in North Korea's western port of Nampo and a $5.8 million project by Taechang Co to produce mineral water in the eastern province of Kangwon.

In the past week, progress has also been made in a project to build nuclear plants in North Korea by the Korean Peninsula Energy Development Organisation (KEDO), an international consortium led by the United States, South Korea and Japan.
KEDO, formed under a landmark 1994 nuclear deal between the United States and North Korea, opened a liaison office earlier this week to oversee the project in the coastal town of Sinpo.
Under the 1994 deal, Pyongyang agreed to abandon its suspected nuclear weapons programme in return for $4.5 billion in nuclear plants and interim energy.
On Wednesday, about 9,000 tonnes of South Korean bulldozers, trucks and heavy equipment arrived in the North to clear land at the site of the project.

In unrelated goodwill gestures, the United States has pledged $52 million and South Korea $16 million in food aid to the hunger-stricken North so far this year. The South Korean Red Cross has also pledged a further $20 million worth of food aid.
